utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-5/18-T, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber is sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Baird being away for urgent personal reasons. Can I have the appearances. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and Iain Reid appear for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all. I have here with me my advisor, Mr. Peter Robinson and Mr. Aleksandar Stevanovic. He looks a bit different, but it is him. He's not wearing a beard anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't recognise him. Thank you for your notice. Yes, for the amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Richard Harvey, still wearing a beard, assisted by Mirjana Vukajlovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Today we are having a Status Conference to review the progress made for the preparation of the Defence case. However, before addressing these issues the Chamber will first deal with a few pending procedural matters. First there are a few exhibit-related matters. The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the accused's request to admit supplemental statements filed on the 30th of August, 2012. In the request the accused asks that the Chamber formally admit into evidence the supplemental statements for Mile Janjic, Milorad Bircakovic, and Ostoja Stanisic, which the Chamber provisionally admitted into evidence on the 25th of June, 2012, and the 29th of June, 2012, respectively, now that the required attestation under Rule 92 bis (B) has been provided for each statement. On the same date, the Prosecution informed the Chamber via e-mail that it will not respond to the request. Having been reviewed, the certified supplemental statements, the Chamber is satisfied that the certification procedure fulfils the formal requirements of Rule 92 bis (B). The Chamber therefore requests the Registry to record that the supplemental statements which have been uploaded into e-court as 1D26311, 1D26312, and 1D26313 are admitted into evidence and to assign exhibit numbers to them. Next, with regard to the Prosecution notice of withdrawal of six exhibits marked for identification, filed confidentially on 29th of August, 2012, the Chamber notes the withdrawal by the Prosecution of the following exhibits marked for identification: P4468, P4550, P4584, P4620, P4819, and P4826. These exhibits shall now be marked by the Registry as not admitted. Finally, the Chamber would also like to take this opportunity to note that there are a number of Prosecution and Defence exhibits which remain provisionally under seal. These include exhibits admitted through, inter alia, Charles Kirudja, KDZ122, KDZ185, and Richard Butler. Therefore, the Chamber instructs the parties to each file a submission by Friday, 14th of September, providing the Chamber with any information relevant to all of their exhibits currently provisionally under seal, including specific requests as to whether each exhibit shall be permanently placed under seal or may be made public. Well, then there are several matters to deal with in private session, so could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now let us discuss some issues regarding the preparation of Defence case. First, I turn to expert reports, Mr. Robinson. The Chamber has received notifications of reports under Rule 94 bis in relation to seven witnesses whom Mr. Karadzic intends to call as expert witnesses. However, with the exception of Derek Allsop's report, the original of which was in English, none of the reports have been translated into English. It should have been clear to you that the Chamber's dead-line of 27th of August required the Defence to produce the expert reports in one of the two official languages of the Tribunal, i.e., English or French. We are now in a situation where the Prosecution cannot possibly start reviewing the reports and will not be able to do so before it receives their English translations. It is only upon its reception that the 30-day response for the Prosecution will run. So, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Robinson, the Chamber would not want this oversight on your part to affect the expeditious conduct of trial and you should have made all efforts for the translations to be ready by the 27th August dead-line. In the meantime you mentioned that all the reports were immediately sent for translation. Could you provide us with a precise update as to when these translations will be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that our case manager has been told by the language section that they will try to have them available by the 5th of November but they can't guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And none of them will be called to testify this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, except Dr. Allsop, whose report is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger or Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have any comments on this? A translation by the 5th of November of these expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the Court is -- thank you, Mr. President, first of all. Yes, as the Court is aware, that is a matter of concern for us as well. We appreciate the Court addressing this so quickly and so firmly. I did not -- I think we did not anticipate that given the volume of the material that CLSS would be in a position to produce all the reports by that date, that is indeed a welcome piece of information. I have actually spoken to Mr. Robinson about this issue earlier. What the Prosecution underscored at that time was that simply deferring the obligations of the Prosecution to respond and the testimony of the individual experts did not fully address the problems created by the untimely submission of the translations because, particularly with respect to the experts related to Sarajevo, it is impossible for us to know what the implications of those untranslated reports may be for the witnesses who are to testify. Therefore, we're quite handicapped in dealing -- or attempting to deal with those particular witnesses. Now, it appears that the impact on the Sarajevo component will be potentially mitigated to some extent by a very early receipt of the reports, if that is indeed feasible. One consideration we would mention at the moment is that if it is CLSS's intention to produce translations of all reports by November 5th, there might be some utility in staggering the translations and prioritising the translation of the Sarajevo-related reports accordingly. So we would need to further consider the witnesses who are intended to be called early against the nature of the reports to the extent we can glean anything about them. But the broader concern that we had which was that it appeared that the Sarajevo expert reports would not be received, at least the translations would not be received, until we were deep into or even concluded with that component, an impossible situation for the Prosecution may not come to pass. So we would like to consider the impact on the Prosecution's case in light of that projected date. We would also ask if the Court -- I don't know if that's an overly sanguine assessment by CLSS and I think to the extent we'll be depending on it, it would be helpful to get some -- for the Trial Chamber to get some confirmation on that. But as I say, we will now reassess the potential impact in accordance with this new information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. In conclusion, I'm urging you, Mr. Robinson and Karadzic, to continue to liaise with CLSS so that English translations can be provided for these expert reports as soon as possible. And the same should apply to the Defence exhibits later on. In the meantime you mentioned that one of the expert reports has already been translated. Which one is that, if you remember, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report relating to air bombs in Sarajevo, modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I note that in relation to Mr. Dusan Dunjic, 65 ter 1D25489 is described on e-court as having been prepared for the Popovic case. That being the case, there must be an English translation available. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a good point, Mr. President. We will look for that. You're probably exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'm now turning to the accused's Rule 65 ter witness list. First thing I would like to raise is the accused's unsworn statement and/or testimony. At paragraph 22 of the Rule 65 ter submissions, the accused mentions that he wishes to make a four-hour unsworn statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis. However, at paragraph 14, he also mentions that he may wish to testify and sets aside 30 hours for that testimony in the 65 ter list. In this regard I wish to first share some guidance about the stage at which the accused decides to give his evidence. It seems to me that the evidence of an accused would carry more weight if it is given right at the beginning of his case rather than later, in light of everything that has been heard, as the accused is the only witness who will have the benefit of hearing all of the others. Thus, Mr. Karadzic, I would simply ask you to carefully consider what I just said. Also, in the event that you do decide to present your evidence first, the Chamber would question the necessity of providing an unsworn statement at all. However, if you were to maintain your request to provide an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis, the Chamber would grant that request but limit your time to one session, namely, one and a half hours. Next, with regard to the issue of witnesses related to sentencing. The accused states in paragraph 4 of the Rule 65 ter submission that he intends to provide a witness and exhibit list for the sentencing phase of trial after the Chamber has called its witnesses, if any, under Rule 98. However, Mr. Robinson, as you know very well, Rule 85 was amended a long time ago back on the 10th of July, 1998, replacing the previous two-stage procedures, i.e., trial and sentencing, by a joint procedure. This means that as a matter of course the Defence Rule 65 ter list must identify witnesses and documents that go to sentencing matters. For Mr. Karadzic not to know this is one thing, but for you, Mr. Robinson, and the rest of the legal team, to me it is unacceptable. So, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, do you wish to comment on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm actually -- I apologise if I should have known that. As I stand here now I'm still of the belief that under Rule 85 we have the right to make that information after the Chamber calls its witnesses. But in terms of disclosure of the information, we're happy to disclose it at any time that the Chamber feels it would be helpful. And if you believe it should be disclosed before the Defence substantive case begins, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now turning to time, I wish to make the following observations. First, for all of the Defence witnesses, except for the testimony of the accused if he wishes to testify himself, the accused lists one hour per witness as the expected time for his examination. However, all of these witnesses, with the exception of a couple, are listed as Rule 92 ter witnesses. The Chamber has reviewed the very few statements which have been uploaded onto e-court. The overwhelming majority of these statements are under ten pages, but the accused still estimates that he will use one hour with these witnesses. Further, for witness 537, I will not mention the name as I am uncertain as to whether or not there are security concerns, there's a 79-page statement and the accused has made one hour for this witness. It thus seems that the Defence has not carefully thought of the time it really needs for each witness. Thus, I wish to remind you, Mr. Karadzic, of the importance of accurate time estimates for witnesses in terms of logistics and planning. As the Rule 65 ter list now stands, these estimates are not useful. I will also remind you of the Chamber's order on the procedure for the conduct of trial issued on 8th of October, 2009, which applied throughout the Prosecution case. In paragraph M of the appendix A, the Chamber ruled that "the presenting party may conduct a limited examination-in-chief of the Rule 92 ter witness where such an examination is focused on clarifying or highlighting particular aspects of the witness's evidence." Therefore, for pure Rule 92 ter witnesses, the Chamber does not envision that they should take more than 30 minutes maximum. Now, as the Prosecution did during its case, the accused may choose to call witnesses as partial Rule 92 ter witnesses, in which case the witness's evidence will be partly submitted in writing and partly elicited orally during direct examination which will not be limited to clarifying or highlighting aspects of that witness's evidence. In the event this is your intention, you must revise your list accordingly so that it accurately reflects the expected status of all the witnesses. Now turning to the subject matter of the witnesses' testimony, although the Chamber will not by principle restrict the witnesses the Defence will call beyond the Chamber's usual and ongoing control over the relevance of the issues presented at trial, I still question the rationale behind the accused calling all of the witnesses listed in his Rule 65 ter list. In particular, I wish to note a few categories of witnesses. First, Tomas Blaszczyk. He was called three times during the Prosecution's case, so it's not clear to me why the accused failed to use Rule 90(H)(i) to elicit information relevant to his case on the three instances when this witness was on the witness-stand, especially during his second appearance in January 2012 when Srebrenica was discussed. Second, there are a lot of witnesses on the list who pertain to municipalities not covered at all by the indictment and barely mentioned in this trial. For the sake of providing you with a non-exhaustive list of such examples, I refer here to witnesses 31 in relation to Ljubinje; 38 in relation to Kozarska Dubica; 114 in relation to Derventa; 116 in relation to Skender Vakuf; 127 in relation to Kupres; 185 in relation to Bosanska Gradiska; and 188 in relation to Bosanski Brod. During the Prosecution's case, Mr. Karadzic, you made a point of moving for the exclusion of evidence pertaining to areas not covered by the indictment and the Chamber granted your request on many occasions. There's no reason why the Chamber should apply a different standard at this stage. Third, similarly there are a number of witnesses pertaining to municipalities for which the indictment only contains very specific allegations related to camps. There is, therefore, no need to present such detailed and repetitive evidence on those municipalities in general as opposed to the camps themselves. So I refer you here to Witnesses 223 in relation to Brcko as well as 219 and 354 in relation to Banja Luka. Also in terms of relevance, I note that you have a lot of witnesses who are expected to provide tu quoque evidence. Throughout the Prosecution case, you were warned by the Chamber that it will not accept such evidence as it has no impact on your responsibility for the crimes alleged in the indictment. Again, I refer you to the following non-exhaustive list of examples: Witnesses 29, 52, 87, 109, 117, 128, 153, 204, and 451, the list would go on. Next, also in terms of relevance, I note that you intend to present detailed and extensive evidence on the attack on the JNA column in Sarajevo through, for instances, Witnesses 66, 250, and 337. Again, this is something that has nothing to do with the crimes alleged in the indictment. Further, there's no need to hear about this event repetitively from several witnesses. I also note your intention to call expert witness on terrorism who will testify about an incident in which part of his family died but which has nothing to do with the indictment. This is Witness 524. Again, I see no point in this witness giving evidence in this trial. Finally, I also want to note that while some of the evidence is of some relevance to the background to this case, there seems to be a lot of unnecessary repetition in the evidence intended to be given by your expected witnesses. I understand that not all of them may ultimately come, but I still question the necessity of even listing so many witnesses who are to give evidence, for example, on the political and historical background and the division of the former Yugoslavia. Again, I will give you a non-exhaustive list of examples and refer you to Witnesses 60, 103, 203, 225, 231, 294, and 398. So, Mr. Karadzic, I have given you a lot of examples of evidence which is irrelevant to your case and of evidence which, even though of some relevance, is far too repetitive. You should also always bear in mind that more evidence you present during your Defence case, the more risk you take that the Prosecution will be able to extract evidence favourable to its case from your witnesses and from documents it may put to your witnesses on cross-examination. Thus, it may be more beneficial to you to be more careful and modest in selecting your witnesses, focusing only on the best witnesses. You will see that applying the guidance will allow you to greatly reduce the number of hours you deem necessary to present your case. So do you wish to comment on the points I referred to, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. Before I ask Mr. Robinson to discuss the legal aspect of this matter, I would like to point out a couple of brief matters myself. I obviously have a different, if not an all together wrong, interpretation of the indictment. I'm now speaking on the basis of your ruling that the responsibility for war is not relevant. I was indicted for formulating the objectives of the Serbian nation which could be achieved only by means of war. The position of the Defence is that those objectives have been achieved before the war by way of political means. So if that is not the case, if I was not indicted for formulating the objectives which led to war, then we should wonder whether I'm -- whether I could be held responsible for anything at all. And it makes me very happy to see that the Chamber doesn't think this to be relevant, but the Prosecution thinks that starting from the autumn of 1991, if not as early as July 1990 when the SDS was established, they claim that our goal was to establish a joint criminal enterprise. And for the same reason, I think it very important to show what actually went on in Yugoslavia, who wanted changes and how those changes came about. It wasn't happening because the Serb side wanted it, especially not the Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not want these major, radical changes in the state fabric of Yugoslavia, and this is something that is stated implicitly in the indictment, that we wanted the war in order to achieve our goals, our objectives. That is not true. The same could be said of municipalities where there were no crimes committed. If you take, for example, a street where there were some crimes and then you omit the entire city, then that looks terrible if that city if representative of the entire town. If I am accused for the systematic approach to committing crimes and so on, that it is important for me to show a pattern because based on that pattern the OTP wanted to include Gorazde, Visegrad, and other municipalities which are not part of the indictment and the Chamber accepted that in order to prove the pattern. Now, if we are talking about the pattern and I am president of the republic and a creator, author of a system, that we should wonder why were there so many municipalities where there was no JCE? Because Republika Srpska has 62 municipalities. So how come this took place in only some municipalities? We heard a witness here, Dr. Mujagic, who said that in areas where they had 20 or 30 per cent there was no problems. So my reading of the indictment is the reason for this attitude of mine, but I think that the OTP has the same reading of the indictment as I do, namely, that at the bottom of the JCE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm going to stop you here. The Chamber does not feel the necessity to repeat all the previous warnings, and you have Mr. Robinson and other legal advisors and you can discuss the distinction between jus in bello and jus ad bellum. So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could Mr. Robinson then present our legal reasons for this stance towards the testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to clarify what Dr. Karadzic is referring to in the decision on the fifth motion for binding order to the United States, the Trial Chamber made the statement that who started the war is not relevant. And he believes, and the witness list reflects, that he's charged with a course of events, a joint criminal enterprise starting in November 1991, in which the expulsion of the population could only have been achieved through force and war. So he believes that the Chamber's ruling that it's not relevant who started the war doesn't comport with his being able to defend that allegation of the indictment. Anyway, I'll leave it at that. With respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And on your part you understand the Chamber's observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand it and I have to tell you I don't agree with them, but that's because I'm a lawyer and not the Judge. So -- but I understand what the Chamber said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: With respect to the rule -- the time estimates, and maybe it would be helpful to clarify that we included in the one hour both the direct examination and anticipated re-direct examination, and we believe that it was prudent to reserve that much time for each witness so that Dr. Karadzic wasn't cut off in the event that the re-direct examination needed to be longer than he anticipated. So that's the reason why we have selected one hour for each of those witnesses. In fact, we expect the direct examination to be very short. In most cases we hope it will be limited to introduction of the statement, if the statement is adequate, and in some cases when Dr. Karadzic meets the witness he may find additional material that he wants to raise with the witness in court, and in that case the witness would be partial 92 ter. So that's the rationale for the time estimate that we gave to the Chamber. And finally with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do understand, Mr. Robinson, that the accurate estimate is also important for in terms of logistics and planning? So that's very important as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And finally with respect to the items of relevance that the Chamber has mentioned, I think we appreciate the Chamber bringing those to our attention and we will take them on board and as the trial develops, just as the Prosecution did with its list, we will be dropping some witnesses who we don't believe have relevant evidence or whose evidence is duplicative of credible evidence that we had managed to bring during the course of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Given all of these issues that I have identified above, I will give the Defence an opportunity to revise its 65 ter witness list so that it includes the accurate time estimate for each witness, the names of the witnesses the Defence may choose to call in relation to sentencing, the accurate status of each witness, and any other amendments necessary in light of my comments above in relation to relevance and repetitiveness. The Defence will have until 14th of September, 2012, in which to file its revised list. Very soon after the Chamber receives the Defence's revised Rule 65 ter list on the 14th of September, the Chamber will issue a decision on the number of hours it allocates for the presentation of the Defence case. But before that, does the Prosecution have any observation to make in relation to the accused's submission that he should be allowed the same amount of time allocated to the Prosecution, i.e., 300 hours, plus an additional 300 hours to rebut the 2 .300 adjudicated facts for which judicial notice has been taken, i.e., in total 600 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would begin by noting that the discussion today I think has highlighted the specious nature of that request all by itself. Secondly, the request for those hours called to mind nothing less than the repetitive requests for huge amounts of cross-examination time based on no particular submissions to the Chamber about what the accused particularly hoped to elicit when the number -- the extraordinary number of hours requested by the accused in those instances were not allocated and were cut back dramatically. The accused nevertheless continued to misuse the amount of time, waste a great deal of time during that process, and only get toward the hard facts toward the very end, and we consider this to be roughly analogous. The accused simply -- he either adopts a figure if not out of thin air then based on some arbitrary mathematical relationship to the amount of time used by the Prosecution without any attempt to indicate to the Court what the basis might be and without any attempt to consider the difference between a Defence case and a Prosecution case with the burden of proving all the facts necessary. That is a distinction which has been highlighted by other Chambers. In short, there are a broad number of factors which were not alluded to in any way by the accused -- in fact, ignored by the accused, including, as the Court indicated today, the amount of time the accused has already used during the course of his cross-examination to elicit matters related to his affirmative Defence case rather than for specific cross-examination of those witnesses. With respect to the patently unfounded and unreasonable attempt to seek double the amount of time used by the Prosecution in its case because of adjudicated facts is no attempt to acknowledge the adversarial nature that went into the establishment of those facts in the first case, no attempt to indicate what facts, if any, the accused considers are necessary to address, no attempt to acknowledge the number -- the overlap between the Prosecution's case and the time it took to perfect that case, and the underlying adjudicated facts and so on. In short, it's a wholly arbitrary figure, very much in keeping with the accused's approach to requested allocations of time for cross-examination and has no more basis than those requests had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Robinson, would you like to reply to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, at paragraph 12 of the Rule 65 ter submission, Mr. Karadzic, you mention that in the event that the Chamber imposes limitations on the Defence case you will seek leave to file additional Rule 92 bis motions. However, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber imposed the same dead-line of 27th of August for filing of both the 65 ter list and the Rule 92 bis motions for a very good reason. As you and your legal advisors must have been aware, the Chamber was expecting you to conduct a thorough review of the evidence you wish to present long before now. Following this review, you were to file Rule 92 bis motions, if any, wherever you thought the Rule 92 bis standard was met and/or to prepare the accompanying Rule 92 bis statements. In other words, the Rule 92 bis motions were not to be used as a counter measure to the Chamber imposing limitations on the time allotted to present your case. Indeed, I remind you that the Prosecution was also requested to file its Rule 92 bis motions prior to the Chamber imposing time-limits on the Prosecution. There's absolutely no reason why the same standard should not apply to your case and you cannot now take it upon yourself to change that dead-line unilaterally. The Chamber, therefore, expects you to do this exercise now and will give you the opportunity to do so no later than Friday, 14th of September, 2012, and to make the appropriate changes to the status of the said witnesses in your revised 65 ter list. Barring exceptional circumstances, the Chamber will not entertain additional Rule 92 bis motions after that date. Now I turn to the timing of production of Rule 92 ter statements. In paragraphs 18 to 20 of the Rule 65 ter submissions, the accused describes the manner in which he plans to organise the finalisation of Rule 92 ter statements and proofing. However, the Chamber is concerned that this schedule is simply not feasible. On the one hand, this system which requires the statement be finalised and signed at least 48 hours prior to the witness's testimony will necessitate the witness to be present in The Hague at least three days prior to the start of his or her testimony. This will be a very heavy logistical burden on the Registry's resources as it will apply to all of the witnesses. It will also be a toll on the witnesses who will have to be staying in The Hague for longer periods of time than what should really be required. I would thus like to hear from the Registry in a Rule 33(B) submission on this matter. So, Mr. Court Officer, if you could immediately send this portion of the transcript to the Registrar so that a Rule 33(B) submission may be filed. Second, while 48 hours may be sufficient in instances where a draft statement as well as associated exhibits have been provided well in advance and when there are very few changes made to the finalised statement during proofing, the Chamber does not consider that is the case when a draft statement has not even been produced yet. It's clear, however, from the 65 ter submission that the Defence has prepared very few such statements at this point and I have grave concerns that the majority will not be prepared until the very last moment. As was the case with the Defence case during the Prosecution's case, the Prosecution should also be given sufficient time to prepare for its cross-examination of the Rule 92 ter witnesses. Furthermore, the Chamber needs sufficient time to make its assessment of the indispensable and inseparable character of the associated exhibits, if any are being tendered. I wish to recall paragraph 1 of the appendix L of the Chamber's order on the conduct of trial of 8th of October, 2009, in which the Chamber had ordered that an amalgamated statement shall be prepared well in advance of the witness arriving in The Hague to testify. It was only in these circumstances that the Chamber had decided that the final amalgamated statement should be provided to the Chamber and the other party no later than 48 hours before the start of testimony. The Chamber again sees no reason to depart from this standard for you, Mr. Karadzic. You have a large team of legal advisors and assistants available to meet with the witnesses and prepare the relevant statements so that these statements can be disclosed to the Prosecution and the Chamber well in advance of their testimony. If during proofing by you or a member of your team minor corrections or changes are made - and I stress the term "minor" - the Chamber takes no issue with the finalised statement being disclosed no later than 48 hours before testimony. This leads me to remind you, Mr. Karadzic, that proofing is not a right and you must understand that it is simply not feasible for you to proof yourself every single one of your witnesses. Not only because you are a self-represented accused but also because this is not feasible, even in cases where the accused are presented by lead counsel and co-counsel where this duty would be split between them. Accordingly, you must be willing to split responsibilities amongst your team members and the Chamber will accept no less from you. While I know that the Registry has been very active in ensuring that mechanisms are in place to accommodate you as much as possible, it is the Chamber's role to ensure that the trial is conducted expeditiously and fairly to all parties involved. I would ask you to think about this, but in the meantime I am requesting you to immediately organise yourself accordingly so that the statements of Rule 92 ter witnesses or partial Rule 92 ter witnesses are prepared and reviewed as soon as possible. So can you tell us where you are in terms of preparing Rule 92 ter statements? Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. So far we have filed 68 statements and our procedure is basically that our investigators are meeting the witness and drafting -- preparing a draft 92 ter statement and will continue to do this so that those are prepared as far in advance as we're able to do that. And the problem is, however, that we don't believe that that statement should be final until Dr. Karadzic has had his input into that because we have investigators who don't know the case that well, haven't been following the proceedings -- in fact, they were just assigned to our team at the end of the Prosecution case. And so we don't feel that a 92 ter statement would be complete without Dr. Karadzic's input. And so we're -- this was our proposal for how best to accommodate all of those concerns, by having a draft statement prepared in the field, disclosing it immediately to the Prosecution, and then once Dr. Karadzic has had his input, making that statement final. But we can't guarantee that that input will only result in minor changes. Dr. Karadzic may know of points or subjects with the witness that the investigator simply didn't know and there may be instances where he adds subjects, not only makes minor corrections. So we're happy to work with the Chamber and the Registry to accept any ideas as to how all of that can be best accomplished. This was our best effort of how we can make these statements available to the Prosecution in draft form at the earliest possible time, while at the same time making sure that the witness's evidence is the best that it can be when it comes to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By Mr. Karadzic's input, do you mean to say that he is intending to proof every and each witness of 92 ter witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't say each witness, but most of the witnesses, the exceptions being some witnesses, international witnesses, for -- who do not wish to come to the Detention Unit and who I have had to do the proofing with myself. But in principle, Dr. Karadzic would like to and believes he's entitled to proof all of the witnesses, just as the Prosecution's attorney who led the witnesses' examination in each and every case for the almost 200 witnesses conducted the proofing of that witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution wish to make any comment on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we both do but let me make a couple of preliminary comments, if I will, just on the facts recently alleged. First of all, I don't think it's factually accurate to say that in each and every case the attorney who led the witness necessarily had a chance to proof him. But more to the point, if -- in the event that there had been a decision by the Prosecution that a single Prosecutor would lead all the witnesses, then that certainly would not have been the case. The Court repeatedly warned the accused that self representation carried that limitation. Secondly, I'm afraid there seems to be a bit of an apples and oranges comparison between proofing and input from the accused. To the extent the accused will be in a position to proof witnesses, we accept that the possibility that additional information, generally we expect of a limited nature, will emerge during that process. But it is difficult to understand why whatever input may inform the taking of a statement cannot be provided well in advance of a proofing session, and so to link those two in the manner that has been done I believe is not a fair characterisation of the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So in producing the Rule 92 ter statements, I would like the Defence to bear in mind what I commented on as well as Mr. Tieger's observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, since we have been discussing proofing, I now wish to turn to the request Mr. Karadzic has made at paragraph 21 of his Rule 65 ter submission, whereby he requests that the Chamber go back to the regular sitting schedule so that he can return to the United Nations Detention Unit by 2.00 p.m. to proof his witnesses. Mr. Karadzic, the extended sitting schedule allowed us to sit for 18 hours per week. If we go back to the regular sitting, four days per week, we would lose more than two hours per week. I understand, however, that you may prefer to have longer afternoons for your preparations. In order for the Chamber not to waste time but also to accommodate your request, we could sit regular sitting hours but do so five days per week. In the end, that would allow us to sit for approximately the same amount of time. I thus give you the option of choosing which of the two options you consider to be the most practical in terms of your preparations. The Chamber is obviously also concerned with preserving your good health, so the Chamber leaves the choice of these two options to you. I think I have exhausted all the items that I prepared for the agenda today, so I'd like to invite the Prosecution and the accused to raise anything if they so wish. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one additional matter, it was on the agenda we provided to the Court earlier, and that relates to the 65 ter summaries. I should mention at the outset that this is a matter that I discussed with Mr. Robinson. As it turns out, it implicates a matter raised by the Court, which is the timing of the submission of the draft statements, a matter that occurred to us as well. In short, it amounts to this: We are concerned with the deficiencies of some of the 65 ter summaries. An example would be something to the effect that the witness will testify about events related to Srebrenica. Clearly, that does not satisfy the Rules requirement for a summary of the facts about which the witness will testify. At the same time, it is theoretically conceivable that the submission -- the timely and early submission of a draft statement may effectively obviate the need for a more fulsome summary to the extent that the Prosecution can be assured that the facts about which the witness will testify will be limited to that statement. And that's a matter I spoke with Mr. Robinson about and indicated to him that we would be happy to work with him, at least for the time being, to see if short of seeking an order from the Court for 65 ter summaries that complied with the Rule, we could reach an accommodation about the timing of the submission of either a draft statement or a finalised statement or a more fulsome and compliant summary. That's what we'll do, reserving the right to return to the Court if and when such an effort proves fruitless and we need then to seek to have the Rule 65 ter complied with in full in accordance with its terms. So that's all I wanted raise. We're trying to work -- we'll try to work it out without involving the Chamber, but should that not prove successful we will return to the Chamber and seek an appropriate order. And finally the only thing that I would add at this point, Mr. President, is that with respect to the reports, the expert reports, we will attempt to liaise with the -- both CLSS and with the Defence in connection with of the impact of the absence of translations on the upcoming witnesses, because I do note that quite a number of them, at least in double figures, would be scheduled to testify before the receipt -- the projected receipt at the earliest time of those reports. So we'll be looking at that. We'll get back to the Court to the extent we learn something that you need to be advised of and that may require some action. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. As regards the issue of the summary and providing a draft statement, I don't see any reason why that cannot be sorted out between the parties. Mr. Robinson, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We appreciate the attitude that the Prosecution has taken and we're committed to working with them to give them as much information about our witnesses as we can. That's the spirit in which we filed these summaries and the submission and in which we've been making available to the Prosecution draft statements and will continue throughout the Defence case to act in that spirit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic, whether the accused is in the position to make his choice as to the format of -- as to the trial schedule.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It certainly would be best if it would be four days until 2.00 p.m.; however, if that option doesn't work, I'd prefer to have longer sitting hours for four days a week, four days is important. I really have to say that all the people who work with me have made a huge effort in order to stick to the schedule. We would have done a lot better if we could have had more time, until the 1st of March, that is. I'm just trying to say that it wasn't arbitrary, the fact that we asked for a dead-line until the 1st of March. I have to say that the people who work for me pro bono and those who are on the list of the Registry worked a huge number of hours each and every day. I would like to thank them for that and I want you to know that we have done our best. We have made every conceivable effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any other matters to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Chamber expects the Defence to file its revised 65 ter list by 14th of September, and the hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: adjourned at 10.26 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
